subject: Automatically identifying nodes where specific evens occur

messages.author: 8fc5adac130f01b8
messages.subject: Automatically identifying nodes where specific evens occur
parts:
Hello all,


I'm trying to get my head around extracting data from results objects. In my study, I have a genus with species spread across a set of islands. I'm specifically interested in questions like is the average age of colonisation from A->B older than B->A. For a single tree this is easy, I can plot my tree with the best biogeographic estimation, figure out which nodes have the desired state change and just use prt() to get the ages of nodes I want. The trick is that I want to do this across a tree sample with changing node numbers to incorporate age variation of estimated trees. Does anybody have a suggestion about how to actually pull this information out of the results object? Is there a way of identifying nodes in a results object where specific state changes occur? I’m guessing it’ll be a combination of the values found in ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node and ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_bottom_below_node but I’m not entirely certain what it is that I would actually do with this.


Any advice would be appreciated.


Many Thanks,


James

Hi all,

So it seems I've misunderstood how the states are encoded in the results object. I had thought that the matrices variously labelled *AT_node* and *below_node* were encoding the state probabilities before and after estimated events (i.e. nodes vs corners) but these always have the same most probable state for all nodes so that can't be what's happening. Instead, I think I need to compare most probable states for each daughter node with each parent node (i.e. what is the most probable state at nodes 10 and 9 and are they states of interest? Does this make sense or am I making this too complicated? If not, does anybody have a suggestion for an automatic way of assigning daughter nodes to their direct parent for example here in the APE/BioGeoBEARS example how would I extract 11 as the parent of tips 1 and 2?

Many Thanks,

James

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Re: Automatically identifying nodes where specific evens occur
parts:
Hi!  For your goals, BSM would be the best option. This will give you a big sample of event histories, and you could query any branch/node of interest and can what the sample of event histories was for that branch/node, and a sample of their timings.

For a sample of different trees, you would have to set up a big loop in R, and either 

(a) run ML on each tree and then BSM on each tree, 

(b) or you could decide to run ML on one tree (maybe the MCC tree) and then take those model parameters and use them for BSM on each tree. 

Option (a) would be somewhat more correct, but probably would make little difference, if the data have strong support for a particular model, and if the tree is reasonably certain.

Option (b) would more fully account for those uncertainties, but would be slower.

Any of these options will require decent skill with for-loops in R, the APE tree structure and prt(), and working with the BSM event tables.

Yet another option is to do the phylogeny and biogeography jointly in RevBayes, there are tutorials on this, but I'm not sure if you can record event histories, and I'm not sure for how big of a problem the runtime is reasonable.

One other note below:

On Wed, Sep 20, 2017 at 8:33 PM, James Kitson <jamesk...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi all,

So it seems I've misunderstood how the states are encoded in the results object. I had thought that the matrices variously labelled *AT_node* and *below_node* were encoding the state probabilities before and after estimated events (i.e. nodes vs corners)

AT_node is the probabilies (or likelihoods or whatever) at the node, which is at a branch top. This point is instantaneously before speciation.  Let's call it node X.

below_node is the probabilities (or likelihoods or whatever) at the BRANCH BOTTOM below that same node X.  This is the same as the corner below node X.  This point is instantaneously after the speciation of node Y, where node Y is the direct ancestor of node X.

All of this is somewhat confusing, but it's all a product of the APE tree structure, where each branch is attached to the node at the top of that branch.  You can use the prt() table to find out which nodes are above or below which other nodes.
but these always have the same most probable state for all nodes so that can't be what's happening.

This shouldn't be true, except for the BAYAREALIKE model or other simple situations (everything living in area A or something).  Probably you are confusing which nodes and corners descend from each other.

Instead, I think I need to compare most probable states for each daughter node with each parent node (i.e. what is the most probable state at nodes 10 and 9 and are they states of interest? Does this make sense or am I making this too complicated? If not, does anybody have a suggestion for an automatic way of assigning daughter nodes to their direct parent for example here in the APE/BioGeoBEARS example how would I extract 11 as the parent of tips 1 and 2?

Many Thanks,

James
